author: Ehsan Salah
title: Why Cairo didn’t turn up for the Quad defense pact party
content:
Standing before cameras on Friday afternoon in the Saudi city of Mecca, the leaders of Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan held up the text of a freshly inked defense pact.

Announcing the pact, Saudi Deputy Public Diplomacy Minister Rayed Krimly said it would allow the three countries “to develop joint defense capabilities, strengthen strategic deterrence, enhance readiness, and further develop and integrate their respective defense capabilities to jointly address any threats to their safety and security.”

“Any external armed attack on any one of the three countries will be considered as an attack on all,” Krimly said, echoing Turkish and Pakistani officials.

Dubbed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, the pact was presented as the capstone of the cooperation among countries that came together to mediate a long-term solution to the United States-led Iran war — which saw Tehran direct swarms of drones and missiles toward neighboring Arab Gulf countries, hit key military and energy installations, and disrupt the shipping of 20 percent of the world’s oil and gas.

Over the last six months, those countries have held meetings in regional capitals, used their diplomatic and economic weight to lobby Iranian and US officials, conveyed backdoor messages, released public statements as a group, and held late night phone calls with one another that were always followed by quick press readou

author: Ahmed Ashmawy
title: Alexandria’s Amreya shuts factory to striking workers
content:
Workers sought intervention from authorities on Sunday after management at Misr al-Amreya Spinning and Weaving Company in Alexandria decided to suspend operations at the factory indefinitely, according to four workers who spoke to Mada Masr.

The management’s statement said the shutdown was to allow for routine maintenance, inventory and reviews. But the workers said they view the move as punishment for their ongoing strike against under-payment.

Hundreds of workers at the company, which is owned by Banque Misr, began a strike in late July, to protest the miscalculation of a “special allowance” bonus to which they are entitled.

The workers told Mada Masr at the time that the company is calculating their bonuses as a percentage of their baseline wages, rather than as a percentage of their insured wages — effectively reducing the bonus value.

The base wage is around a third of the value of the insured wage, as per a worker’s payslip that Mada Masr reviewed last month.

A new social insurance law ratified in July obliges public sector companies to pay a “special allowance” bonus and to calculate it at the rate of 12 percent of the insured wage. Worker representatives speaking to Mada Masr last week said that the company owner has said Amreya is a private company exempt from the requirement, but the head of the company’s workers union committee, Mohamed al-Sawy, told Mada Masr t

author: Salma Abdelrahman
title: Open call for proposals and reporting practices on artificial intelligence
content:
Everything is about AI now. On a general discourse level, a prophecy is being shoved down our throats telling us it is the one thing that is going to fundamentally change life as we know it.

The prophecy comes at us wrapped in the language of utopia and a tech giant’s latest market offering. Today, the capabilities of the computational power behind AI models are unprecedented, so much so that it may very well rival the cognitive skills of the human mind. AI is going to solve the mysteries of disease and eradicate world poverty, we are told. Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, has declared the arrival of “singularity,” the concept of machine intelligence surpassing human intelligence, two times now and still counting. Demis Hassabis, the CEO of Google’s DeepMind, is the more cautious one: he only promises we are “near” it.

Based on these claims, hundreds of billions of dollars of capital are being thrown into AI-related investments, roughly 1 percent of global GDP. That is not counting the overall compulsion of businesses from all over the world to switch to AI, mainly out of fear of missing out on something big.

The implications are profound. Fantasies of replacing human labor that have been the obsession of capitalism for the past two centuries are reaching new heights with AI’s support. Data centers are being erected everywhere, doubling the global demand for copper. Operating

The military’s offensive in Kordofan continued this week with the capture of the strategic Jabal al-Dayer area near Rahad, building on last week’s gains that brought five towns and the Saderat Road linking Khartoum and Kordofan back under military control.

Military sources told Mada Masr the latest advance consolidates the military’s hold over southern and western North Kordofan while placing key routes into Rapid Support Forces-held areas in South Kordofan and West Kordofan under its control.

A senior military officer said that air strikes on remaining RSF positions in North Kordofan over the past week are also part of preparations for a simultaneous advance into the neighboring state.

Along the Chadian border, the RSF launched successive attacks on Bir Saliba and Hagar al-Marfaeen in West Darfur this week, but the military and allied forces repelled the assault after more than 12 hours of fighting. The area forms a key cross-border supply corridor linking the military’s positions in West Darfur with its operational bases in North Darfur.

In South Kordofan, a years-long dispute between the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North — the RSF’s ally led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu — and one of its oldest constituencies, the Otoro tribe, has reached the movement’s seat of power.

author: Roaa Reda
title: The dilemma of the ‘undeserving’: Families cut off from food subsidies describe prohibitively complex appeal process
content:
Walaa Mahdi, a resident of a Cairo neighborhood, is among the hundreds of thousands of people across the country who have found their government ration cards suddenly suspended this summer.

The smart card normally gives her and her family access to a basket of household essentials at state-subsidized prices: they get sugar, rice and oil via the card, as well as a daily quota of subsidized loaves.

When her card was suspended, she went to the local supply office to check its status. There, she discovered that her card was suspended on the grounds that her youngest son is enrolled in a private high school.

Mahdi was shocked by the suspension. The school is not a luxury for her son, but a hard-won investment their family is making in his education. They will pay the annual fee in installments, and her son is working alongside his studies to pay for the education. “How can this mean I am ‘underserving’ of support?” she wonders, speaking to Mada Masr.

Mahdi is not alone. She is one of at least 850,000 people the state has expelled from the subsidy program since June in a campaign it is pitching as “purifying operations” to rid the subsidy database of “undeserving” beneficiaries to improve the targeting of government resources.

author: Mahmoud Bashir
title: Mass funeral held for 112 people whose bodies were recovered from single Gaza residential block bombed by Israel
content:
Thousands of Palestinians gathered in Gaza City on Tuesday to bury 112 people, including 40 children, from the Abu Sharia and Hassaineh families.

Their bodies were recovered over the past weeks from beneath the ruins of their homes in the Sabra neighborhood in southern Gaza City, which Israel bombed without warning during the second month of its 2023 war on the enclave, according to Gaza’s Civil Defense Directorate.

In one of the largest mass funerals held in Gaza, the bodies and remains, draped in Palestinian flags, were placed near the families’ destroyed homes. After funeral prayers, they were buried in the Zeitoun neighborhood’s Baptist cemetery in southeastern Gaza City.

The strike on the residential block in November 2023 is believed to have killed around 153 people.

Work to recover the 112 bodies began in July, but shortages of equipment and personnel made the process arduous, Civil Defense spokesperson Mahmoud Basal told Mada Masr. The bodies of the remaining 41 people were not recovered.

The victims are among nearly 14,000 people missing since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and believed to be trapped under the rubble, he said.

The operation began in mid-July and relied on a single excavation vehicle, which the agency obtained  with support from the International Committee of the Red Cross.

author: Sara Seif Eddin
title: Damietta drone strike underscores precarity of Egypt’s ‘regional hub’ ambitions after energy link-up to Cyprus
content:
A new link-up between natural gas fields in Cyprus and processing facilities in Egypt was greenlit last week, with European energy giants TotalEnergies and Eni taking their final investment decision to fund the project.

The deal will allow for natural gas produced in Cyprus to be liquefied and exported from Egypt’s Mediterranean coast by 2028, a step that TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanné said would bolster “Europe’s energy security.” The bloc’s main natural gas suppliers have been hit in recent months by the disruption that the United States’ war on Iran has wrought on regional energy markets, as well as by ongoing tensions over the four-year war in Ukraine.

More importantly for Egypt, the long-awaited investment brings the country a step closer to fulfilling its ambition to become “a regional energy hub” — a policy target that successive governments have failed to hit since its adoption in 2018 .

Sources previously speaking to Mada Masr have described the Cyprus deal as a route to soothing Egypt’s energy deficit and, consequently, its dependence on Israeli gas imports, which have proved a source of diplomatic tensions in recent years adding to existing friction over Israel’s wars in the region.

The link-up also holds major potential to bolster Egypt’s foreign currency inflows from its Mediterranean coast, adding to existing revenue from Red Sea shipping, former Suez Cana

author: Mostafa Hosny
title: Egyptian Drug Authority studies new flexible pricing system as pharmaceutical companies push for increases
content:
A new formula that would allow more frequent medicine price fluctuations is under review by the Egyptian Drug Authority (EDA), according to four informed sources who spoke to Mada Masr.

An EDA official and the head of a pharmaceutical company who spoke to Mada Masr on condition of anonymity said the EDA, which is responsible for setting prices nationwide, is looking into the system against the backdrop of repeated disputes with pharmaceutical companies requesting price increases.

Drug prices have spiraled in recent years as the pound has weakened against the dollar and raw materials costs have increased accordingly.

Yassin Ragai, the assistant to the EDA’s head, told Mada Masr that the drug authority held meetings this month with various stakeholders in the pharmaceutical industry to discuss the new mechanism in light of various pressures on the drug market in recent years.

Ragai said the meetings came amid a desire to encourage further investments in the pharmaceutical sector “through a clear and transparent formula and a publicly announced, up-to-date mechanism.”

The last amendment to the pricing system took place in 2012, said Ragai. That mechanism, established by Health Ministerial Decree 499/2012, mandated that drug price reviews should take place based on fluctuations of 15 percent or more in the exchange rate. author: Sarah Mahfouz, Sara Seif Eddin, Ehsan Salah, Hazem Tharwat, Mohamed Abdel Khaleq
title: The Damietta drone: A night of caution and speculation
content:
After a night of speculation, the Egyptian Cabinet said on Thursday morning that the fire that broke out aboard two energy vessels at Damietta Port the day before was caused by a drone strike, though it did not disclose who launched the drone.

A worker at the port who witnessed the incident says they heard a massive explosion at 2:10 pm on Wednesday. The blast occurred at berth 27, at the far end of the port near an area known as the silos zone, close to the facilities of SEGAS , the company that operates the Damietta liquefaction plant.

Police immediately sealed off the site and established a security cordon, the witness tells Mada Masr. “No extra security measures happened , and nobody had their phones taken. They cordoned off the berth. Ambulances arrived, but none left carrying casualties. They just closed off the area and we carried on with our workday as normal,” they say.

Two parliamentary sources speaking to Mada Masr confirm that the incident occurred at around 2:30 pm. Vessel traffic at the port was subsequently suspended until the affected ship had been towed out of the port basin. After 6 pm, navigation resumed, the sources say, which was confirmed by the Damietta Port Authority in a statement on Thursday.

author: Mostafa Hosny
title: Cracks in the Universal Health Insurance system: An accounting of phase 1
content:
In the government’s telling, the first phase of the Universal Health Insurance rollout was a success . And with that success in hand, it says now that the scheme is ready to expand.

Six years ago, people in Port Said, Ismailia, Suez, South Sinai, Luxor and Aswan — the first governorates to see the rollout of the 2018 law  — were brought into the new system.

The promise was something better than the old model, a healthcare system built on social solidarity. People would pay less out of pocket. They would find a place in hospitals. Medicines and treatment would be there when they needed them.

But patients across those six governorates who spoke to Mada Masr over recent months describe months-long shortages of critical medicines and medical devices and appointment scheduling bottlenecks. Many, who were enrolled in the program whether they wanted to join or not, are now being effectively denied healthcare over unpaid insurance contributions that have climbed in some cases into the tens of thousands of pounds.

“All we hear is that the system is a success, but what we see is something completely different,” says a resident of Aswan. What is on the ground is a service well below even the minimum standard, he says.

The problems in the first phase were not unforeseen. Several officials and health policy experts involved in the drafting of the law at the time tell Mada Masr that the

author: Mada Masr
title: Fire at Damietta Port energy facilities brought under control, says Petroleum Ministry, without comment on cause
content:
A fire broke out at natural gas facilities in the Damietta Port on Wednesday afternoon, the Petroleum Ministry said in a statement , without elaborating on the cause of the incident.

Maritime security firm Ambrey said that a drone struck a United States-owned LNG floating storage facility and a Greek-owned LNG tanker at the port, causing a fire that the security firm said was brought under control.

The Petroleum Ministry affirmed in its statement that there were no injuries or fatalities as a result of the fire, urging media outlets and social media users to refer to official statements issued by the ministry for further information.

The ministry said that the fire had broken out on a regasification vessel and a storage vessel in the port.

Damietta is a key energy logistics site, hosting natural gas facilities that serve Egypt’s export and import needs.

Regasification and storage vessels are currently stationed in its port to facilitate Egypt’s use of imported energy cargo to power homes and industries across the country.

Reuters cited trade sources to report that the vessel that had been struck is Energos Winter, a storage and regasification unit that sails under a Marshall Islands flag that was contracted by Egypt’s government to Damietta Port last year to support Egypt’s gas import processing.

The trade sources and energy sources said the cause of the fire was a drone

author: Mahmoud Bashir, Thaer Abu Aoun, Omar Moussa
title: Cashless economy forced on Gaza to detriment of Palestinians
content:
Reliance on banking apps and e-wallets has surged in recent weeks in Gaza, despite the strip’s lack of the infrastructure needed to support such a shift. 




While vendors see digital transfers as a solution to Gaza’s cash shortage crisis, unreliable internet service, prolonged power outages and recurring technical problems with banking apps and e-wallets frequently prevent transactions from going through, according to residents and vendors who spoke to Mada Masr.




A Palestinian economist told Mada Masr that the crisis created by the unreliability of electronic transactions is the result of a deliberate Israeli policy aimed at engineering a distorted economic reality in Gaza.




Gaza began moving to a cashless economy at the end of last year. After Israeli authorities stopped accepting cash payments from Gaza’s merchants, vendors followed suit. Gaza already faced a lack of small denominations and a shortage of cash — much of the currency in circulation has deteriorated, and no new banknotes have entered the strip since the beginning of the war and the tightening of the Israeli siege. But once Israel changed its payment method, many vendors now exclusively accept digital transactions.  




Before the war, Gaza was 

served 

by around 11 banks, six Palestinian and five foreign. Only their mobile apps remained accessible after all 56 bank branches shut down during the war.

With Washington’s revised ceasefire initiative drawing cautious engagement from Khartoum and diplomatic activity around Sudan intensifying, much of the week’s political maneuvering both abroad and at home revolved around preparing for a possible new phase of negotiations.




In Asmara, Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan held lengthy talks on July 17 with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, one of his closest regional allies.




Ceasefire proposals dominated the meeting. Burhan reiterated Khartoum’s insistence that any truce must be preceded by a Rapid Support Forces withdrawal from cities, a position Afwerki doubled down on, a Sudanese diplomat informed of the discussions said. The two leaders have long aligned around preserving state institutions and rejecting political arrangements that elevate armed groups alongside them.




Security cooperation followed. The two sides agreed to deepen military and intelligence coordination, a Sudanese security source said. They also discussed Red Sea security as concerns grow that the United States-Iran war could spill into the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

author: Jeffrey G. Karam
title: When Egypt tried to build its own missile program
content:
What happens when a postcolonial state attempts to challenge the global concentration of advanced technology? From artificial intelligence to nuclear technology and advanced weapons, this question has once again moved to the center of global politics. Yet the struggle over who possesses advanced knowledge, who is permitted to develop it and who claims the authority to deny it to others has a much longer history.




On July 23, 1962, exactly 10 years after Egypt’s revolution, former President Gamal Abdel Nasser offered his own answer. Rockets rose over the Egyptian desert as Egypt marked the anniversary of the 1952 revolution. Nasser declared that the country had entered the missile age.




The spectacle reflected ambitions that extended well beyond the missiles themselves. Emerging from colonial rule and repeated military defeats, Egypt sought to demonstrate that it could acquire and produce advanced technologies long-monopolized by the industrialized world. For Nasser, the missile program was not simply about military power. It formed part of a broader project of technological sovereignty: the belief that political independence remained incomplete without the capacity to master modern science and industry.




The response quickly became international. Israeli intelligence launched a covert campaign against the German scientists helping build the program through intimidation

author: Moataz Hagag
title: The unregulated crocodile
content:
In June, people in Hasafa village in Qalyubiya shared photos and videos on social media of a small crocodile, about a meter long, roaming through a drainage canal. A team from the Environment Ministry was dispatched to catch it, and the ministry later 

said 

the crocodile would be taken to Aswan and released into its “natural habitat in Lake Nasser.”




A few days later, another larger crocodile was 

spotted 

sliding from a muddy bank into an irrigation canal near the village of Shabramant in Aboul Nomros in Giza. Again, an Environment Ministry team 

located

 it and transferred it to one of the ministry’s facilities.




The successive sightings of Nile crocodiles so far north along the river raises questions over how they got there. Since the Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970, the species has been found almost exclusively in Lake Nasser, as changes to their natural habitat had already reduced their movement beyond the lake.







In its statement about the Hasafa crocodile, the ministry suggested that someone had thrown the animal into the canal, pointing to the illegal possession and trade of crocodiles. Ekramy al-Abassiry, the general director of the South Egypt sector of protected areas and the head of the Crocodile Management Unit at the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency in Aswan, offers the same explanation. author: Thaer Abu Aoun, Omar Moussa
title: Israel expands occupied zone in Gaza City’s Zeitoun, orders evacuations in Deir al-Balah
content:
Israel extended the area under its control along Gaza’s eastern edge earlier this week, carrying out military operations in Gaza City and Deir al-Balah that forced people into displacement, eyewitnesses in both cities told Mada Masr.




The two governorates lie adjacent to the “yellow line” established under the October ceasefire agreement, marking the zone that has remained under Israeli occupation. In recent months, Israeli forces have gradually pushed beyond that line, issuing evacuation orders farther west ahead of military advances.




In Gaza City’s southeastern Zeitoun neighborhood, the Israeli military began operations on Saturday with heavy artillery shelling that forced dozens of families to flee westward, an eyewitness who lives in the neighborhood told Mada Masr.




Military vehicles then advanced into eastern Zeitoun as far as Salah Eddin Road, bringing the Dawla and Mostawsaf areas within the occupied zone.




After forcing residents to leave, the military “immediately began targeting anyone entering the area,” the eyewitness said.




Two residents of Zeitoun said shelling continued over the next two days, driving further displacement. Early Sunday, three people were killed and several others injured when Israeli shelling hit a gathering of civilians on Kashko Street near the Dawla junction in southern Zeitoun, the residents told Mada Masr.

author: Amira El-Fekki
title: Sayed Moshagheb trial over homecoming celebration postponed by terrorism court
content:
A Cairo special terrorism court postponed on Monday the trial of former Ultras White Knights leader Sayed Fahim, known as Sayed Moshagheb, and five others to September 22.  




The session was the first in the case against Moshagheb and his friends, who are facing charges of unlawful assembly and possession of fireworks over a gathering they held to celebrate his release after nearly 11 years in detention.




The defense team submitted several procedural requests before the court, including hearing witnesses and presenting evidence, defense lawyer Osama al-Gohary told Mada Masr.




Moshagheb was released on April 16 after spending over a decade detained in connection with the 2015 Air Defense Stadium case and a subsequent case with the State Security Prosecution. 




Hours after his release, following a spontaneous gathering organized by friends outside his home in Bulaq al-Dakrour, he and five others were 

rearrested

.




The Interior Ministry had 

described

 the celebration of Moshagheb’s release as a “riot,” where fireworks were launched and traffic was disrupted in the Giza neighborhood, “causing public alarm.”

author: Rana Mamdouh, Sara Seif Eddin
title: Ahramat al-Nil: Egypt’s new sovereign fund
content:
A law restructuring the Future of Egypt for Sustainable Development Authority, 

approved 

by Parliament last week, establishes a new sovereign fund with special status, the Ahramat al-Nil fund, which will report directly to the authority and, in turn, the presidency.




The fund joins the authority’s “

sustainable development zones

” and a second service fund, Daem, as one of the three primary mechanisms through which Future of Egypt will carry out its expansive mandate.




The law’s second chapter sets out the regulations governing the new fund. It describes Ahramat al-Nil as the authority’s investment arm, tasked with “achieving sustainable economic development, maximizing the value of investment assets for future generations and strengthening the economy in the face of crises.”




The fund is part of efforts to channel state assets and wealth into investment through sovereign entities operating across sectors including energy, infrastructure, tourism, education and healthcare, both directly and in partnership with private investors. However, the fund itself expands the exceptional position that Future of Egypt has come to occupy through both the new law and the way the authority has operated since its inception. This exceptional position allows the fund to operate more freely, compared to the existing state apparatus and its internal, sometimes contradictory, mandates

author: Rana Mamdouh
title: Future of Egypt: ‘A law that regulates the absence of law’
content:
After operating for over four years without a declared legislative framework, the House of Representatives gave final approval on Tuesday to a bill reorganizing the Future of Egypt for Sustainable Development Authority.




The executive branch submitted the bill to Parliament on July 6, which included a proposal to transfer the authority’s oversight from the Defense Ministry to the president.




It was then referred to a joint parliamentary committee comprising the Constitutional and Legislative Affairs Committee and the bureaus of the chamber’s other committees, which met on July 8 and 9.




The committee introduced amendments and added new provisions before sending the draft to the plenary session, where debate began on Tuesday and concluded with its final passage on Wednesday, in the presence of the authority’s executive director Colonel Bahaa al-Ghannam.




The bill grants the authority sweeping powers, effectively allowing it to replace most state administrative bodies operating within what it defines as “sustainable development zones,” while also empowering it to consolidate and manage state-owned assets.




A source close to both the government and Parliament tells Mada Masr that the draft law had been sent from the presidency to the government without being reviewed by the Cabinet’s advisory council, the body responsible for examining all government-sponsored legis

author: Shams Eddin Essam
title: Future of Egypt enters domestic fertilizer retail market
content:
The first fertilizer stock to be supplied by the Future of Egypt for Sustainable Development Authority was distributed on Monday for sale through agricultural cooperatives across the country

.

Fertilizer distribution adds yet another market to the fast-expanding portfolio in which the Future of Egypt authority has an arm.

The authority has signed open-ended supply agreements with the cooperatives, which are to distribute the fertilizer to farmers across governorates at prices below those on the open market.

Cooperatives are typically responsible for distributing government-subsidized fertilizer to farmers under a decades-old scheme backed by the Agriculture Ministry. But the ministry is not involved in the Future of Egypt distribution scheme for unsubsidized fertilizer, an official from the cooperatives told Mada Masr.

Instead, Future of Egypt procures fertilizer from manufacturers and supplies it to the cooperatives, which sell it to farmers on its behalf at prices the authority has set.

Under the agreement, Future of Egypt will undercut the standard market prices. A sack of unsubsidized urea will be sold for no more than LE1,000 and ammonium nitrate for LE975, compared with the current open-market rates of between LE1,400-1,600 per sack.
